content:
To sell personalised products online, your store needs four things that a normal product page does not have: clear personalisation fields (text, font, colour, photo upload) with limits shown up front, a preview that shows the customer roughly what they will receive, a price that updates as options are chosen, and a way for the personalisation details to travel cleanly from the cart to the order, the invoice and the production team. For anything expensive or complex, add a proof-approval step before production. On Shopify this is usually built with line item properties and a personalisation app; on WooCommerce with a product add-ons extension; on a custom build with your own option model. For ecommerce website development in Pune we see this most often with gifting brands, printing businesses, jewellers, stationery makers, bakeries and corporate merchandise suppliers, and the same problems come up every time: names spelt wrong, photos too low-resolution to print, and orders where nobody can find what the customer actually typed.

This guide is for owners of stores that sell, or want to sell, made-to-order or personalised items: engraved gifts, name-printed apparel, custom cakes, photo frames, wedding stationery, branded corporate kits. It explains how to design the product page, which platform approach fits, how to handle uploads and proofs, and what to state in your policies.

## Why personalised products need a different product page

A standard product page answers "Is this the right item, in the right size, at the right price?" A personalised product page must also answer:

- What can I change, and what can't I?
- How will my name, message or photo actually look?
- What happens if I make a typo?
- How long will it take, given that it is made after I order?
- Can I return it if I don't like it?

If the page doesn't answer these, customers either abandon the purchase or fill your WhatsApp with questions. Both are expensive. And the operational side is less forgiving than for stock items: if the personalisation text is lost or misread between the website and the workshop, you have made a product nobody else can buy.

## Types of personalisation and what each needs

Before choosing tools, list exactly what customers can personalise. Most stores use a combination of these:

### Text

Names, initials, dates, short messages. Needs: a character limit that matches the physical space, allowed characters (can they use emoji, Devanagari, Marathi?), case handling (will "ananya" be printed as typed or capitalised?), and sometimes a line-count limit.

### Font, colour and placement

A choice of three to six fonts, thread or ink colours, and position (left chest, back, sleeve). Needs: visual swatches rather than font names alone, and rules about which combinations are allowed.

### Photo or file upload

Photos for frames, mugs, cushions, cake toppers; logo files for corporate merchandise. Needs: accepted file types, minimum resolution for the print size, maximum file size, cropping guidance and a rights confirmation.

### Configured products

Products built from components: a gift hamper with chosen items, a custom cake with flavour, size, tiers and message, a kit with a choice of colours per item. Needs: dependent options (if two tiers, then these flavours), quantity rules and price rules.

### Made-to-measure

Tailored clothing, curtains, furniture. Needs: measurement fields with units, guidance diagrams and validation. This overlaps with the sizing guidance we cover in our article on [size charts, variants and fit guides](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-size-charts-variants-fit-guides-2026).

The more of these you combine, the more likely you need custom development rather than an off-the-shelf add-on.

## Designing the personalisation fields

### Show limits before the customer types

Tell customers the rules next to the field, not in an error after they submit:

- "Up to 12 characters including spaces. Letters A–Z and numbers only."
- "Upload a JPG or PNG, at least 1,800 × 1,200 pixels for best print quality."

Show a live character counter for text fields. If the item physically cannot fit more than a certain number of characters at a readable size, enforce that limit in the field rather than accepting long text and failing later.

### Make the field labels specific

"Personalisation" is vague. "Name to engrave on the front" and "Message for the gift card (not printed on the product)" are clear. Many mistakes we see come from customers typing a gift message into the engraving field.

### Ask for confirmation of spelling

Add a simple check below important text fields: "Please check spelling, spacing and capital letters. We print exactly what you type." A required tick box ("I have checked my personalisation") reduces errors without adding much friction. Some stores show the text back in a confirmation step in the cart.

### Handle Indian languages properly

If you allow names in Devanagari or other scripts, test that your fonts, preview, order emails, invoice PDFs and production files all render the text correctly. Complex scripts can render incorrectly in some PDF and label generators even when they look fine on the website. If your production process cannot handle a script, do not allow it in the field.

### Keep optional and required fields clear

Mark which fields are required. If the product can be bought without personalisation, make that the default and label the personalisation section as optional, with the extra price shown.

## Showing a preview

A preview reduces uncertainty, which reduces both abandoned carts and returns. There are three levels, with very different costs.

### Level 1: example images

Photos of real finished products with different names and fonts, plus a clear font sample image. Cheap, and often enough for simple engraving or embroidery. Take these photos yourself; do not use mock-ups that show finishes you cannot achieve. Our guide to [product photography briefs and image specs](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-product-photography-video-brief-shot-list-image-specs-2026) covers how to plan these shots.

### Level 2: live text preview

The customer's text is drawn over a product image in the chosen font and colour as they type. This is achievable with most personalisation apps and with modest custom development. It is not a production proof; label it "Preview: final placement and size may vary slightly".

### Level 3: full product designer

A canvas where customers move, resize and rotate text and images, choose backgrounds and see the result on several views of the product. Common for print-on-demand and corporate merchandise. It is expensive to build well, heavy on mobile and needs careful testing. Choose this only if customers genuinely need that much control.

Whatever the level, make sure the preview works on a phone, where most shoppers browse. A designer tool that is usable only on desktop will lose most mobile visitors.

## Pricing personalisation

Customers should never see a surprise at checkout. Common pricing models:

- **Flat fee per personalisation:** for example, a fixed charge for engraving any name up to the limit.
- **Per character or per line:** for longer messages.
- **Per option:** extra for a premium font, a second position, or gift wrapping.
- **Percentage of product price:** less common, harder to explain.

Show the personalisation price next to the field, update the total on the product page as options change, and show a breakdown in the cart. On WooCommerce, the official Product Add-Ons extension lets an option add a flat fee, a fee per quantity or a percentage. On Shopify, per-option pricing usually needs an app, because line item properties on their own do not change the price.

## How personalisation travels through the order

This is where most problems arise. The customer's choices must appear, unchanged, in every place someone needs them.

### Cart and checkout

Show each personalisation detail under the item in the cart, with an "Edit" link that takes the customer back to the product with their entries intact. Two identical products with different names must appear as separate cart lines, not merge into one line with quantity two.

### Order confirmation and emails

Repeat the personalisation in the order confirmation page and email, so the customer has a second chance to spot a typo. Include a clear line: "Spotted a mistake? Reply within 2 hours" or whatever window your production schedule allows. We cover the wider setup of confirmation pages and emails in our guide to [order confirmation pages and transactional emails](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-order-confirmation-page-transactional-emails-2026).

### Admin, invoice and packing slip

Your team needs to see personalisation without opening each order. Check that:

- The order screen shows all personalisation fields clearly, not as cryptic internal keys.
- Uploaded files are linked from the order and downloadable at full resolution.
- The invoice shows that the item is personalised, without necessarily reproducing every detail.
- The packing or production slip shows everything the workshop needs.

On Shopify, personalisation captured as line item properties is stored with the order. Property names that begin with an underscore are conventionally hidden from the customer at checkout, which is useful for internal data such as a preview image URL, but make sure your team can still see them in the admin.

### Production export

For more than a handful of orders a day, copying details by hand is slow and error-prone. Set up an export, a production sheet or a direct integration that lists each personalised item with its fields and file links. For engraving and printing, some businesses generate a production-ready file automatically from the customer's input. That is custom work, but it pays for itself quickly at volume.

## Handling photo and file uploads

### Resolution and file checks

Low-resolution photos are the most common cause of disappointing printed products. Set a minimum pixel size based on the print size and print quality you need, and check it in the browser on upload. If an image is below the minimum, warn the customer clearly before they proceed rather than silently accepting it. Accept common formats (JPG, PNG, and HEIC from iPhones if your tool can convert it), and set a sensible maximum file size so uploads work on mobile data.

### Cropping

If the product has a fixed shape (square frame, round coaster), let customers crop to that shape and see the result. Otherwise your team will crop it, and the customer may not like what is cut off.

### Storage, privacy and rights

Customer photos often show family members, including children. Treat them as personal data:

- Store uploads in a private location that only your team can access, not in a public folder with guessable URLs.
- State in your privacy policy what you collect, why and how long you keep it, and delete uploads after a defined period once the order is complete and any return window has passed.
- Ask customers to confirm they have the right to use the image. For logos and artwork, that means confirming they own or are licensed to use the brand.
- Restrict which staff can download originals.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act and the DPDP Rules notified in November 2025 set out obligations for businesses that process personal data, with most operational rules phased in over eighteen months. If uploads are a core part of your business, have your privacy notice and retention practices reviewed.

### Upload security

File uploads are a common attack route. Allow only the file types you need, check files on the server (not just by their extension), store them outside the web root or in object storage, and never execute or render uploaded files on your own pages without processing them. Any reputable app or developer should handle this; ask how.

## Proof approval for high-value or complex orders

For wedding cards, corporate merchandise with logos, large prints and expensive engraving, a proof step protects you and the customer:

1. The customer places the order and pays, or pays a deposit if that is your policy.
2. Your team prepares a digital proof showing the final layout.
3. The customer receives the proof by email or WhatsApp with a link to approve or request changes.
4. Production starts only after approval, and the approval is recorded on the order with the date and time.

Set a limit on revision rounds, state what counts as a change versus a correction of your error, and explain what happens if the customer does not respond. Show the proof step and its effect on delivery time on the product page so it is not a surprise.

If you send proofs and status updates on WhatsApp, use approved message templates through the WhatsApp Business Platform and keep the conversation linked to the order.

## Lead times and delivery promises

Personalised items take longer to dispatch than stock items. On the product page, show production time separately from delivery time: "Made in 2–3 working days, then dispatched." In the cart and checkout, if you show an estimated delivery date, make sure it includes production time. For festival and wedding-season orders, show a clear cut-off date for delivery before a specific day, and update it as the date approaches.

## Returns, cancellations and what to state

Personalised products cannot usually be resold, so many stores restrict returns on them. India's Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 require e-commerce entities to display return, refund, exchange, warranty, delivery and cancellation information clearly. So:

- State your policy for personalised items on the product page, in the cart and in your returns policy, not only in the footer.
- Distinguish between change of mind (often not accepted for personalised items) and products that are defective, damaged or do not match what was ordered (which you must still put right).
- State until when an order can be cancelled or edited, for example "until production starts" or "within 2 hours of ordering".

Take legal advice on the exact wording of your returns policy; this article explains what the website needs to show, not what your legal obligations are in every case.

## Platform options

### Shopify

Shopify captures personalisation on the product form as line item properties, which are stored with the order. Basic text fields can be added in the theme. For file uploads, conditional options, live previews and option pricing, most stores use a personalisation or product options app. Check how the app stores files, whether uploads survive any express checkout buttons your theme shows, how it affects page speed, and what happens to your data if you stop paying for it.

### WooCommerce

The official WooCommerce Product Add-Ons extension supports text fields with character limits, multiple-choice options, file uploads and option pricing (flat, per quantity or percentage). For conditional logic, WooCommerce recommends combining Gravity Forms with its product add-ons extension, and several third-party plugins offer similar features. Because WooCommerce runs on your own server, you control where uploaded files are stored, which helps with privacy and retention.

### Custom build

A custom option model, preview and production export make sense when personalisation is central to the business, when options depend on each other in complex ways, or when you want proofs, production files and order data in one system. It costs more up front, but avoids stacking several apps that each own part of the order.

## Budget and timeline ranges

These are indicative ranges for planning, not quotes:

- **Adding simple text personalisation and example images** to an existing store: often a few days of setup and testing, plus any app subscription.
- **Live text preview, file upload with resolution checks and option pricing** using an app or extension: roughly one to three weeks including configuration, design adjustments and testing.
- **Custom personalisation module with proof approval and production export:** typically several weeks to a few months, depending on the number of product types and integrations.

App and extension prices change, so check current pricing before budgeting. TODO: add Govindani's current package pricing for personalisation setups once confirmed by the sales team.

## Testing checklist before you launch

- [ ] Every personalisation field has a clear label, limit and example
- [ ] Character limits enforced in the field, and long names tested at the real physical size
- [ ] Devanagari or other scripts either work end to end or are blocked
- [ ] Preview works on a small Android phone and on iPhone
- [ ] Low-resolution image triggers a clear warning
- [ ] Price updates correctly for every option combination
- [ ] Two of the same product with different names stay as separate cart lines
- [ ] Personalisation appears in cart, confirmation page, email, admin order and production slip
- [ ] Uploaded files download at full resolution from the order
- [ ] Returns and cancellation rules for personalised items are visible before purchase
- [ ] Uploads are stored privately and deleted on schedule

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I add a personalisation option to my online store?

On Shopify, add text fields as line item properties in your theme or use a product personalisation app for uploads, previews and option pricing. On WooCommerce, use a product add-ons extension. Show limits next to each field, update the price as options change, and check that the details appear in the cart, confirmation email and admin order.

### Can customers upload photos when ordering on my website?

Yes. Both Shopify, through apps, and WooCommerce, through add-on extensions, support file uploads with the order. Set accepted formats, a minimum resolution for the print size and a maximum file size, store uploads privately and delete them after a defined period.

### Should personalised products have a live preview?

A preview reduces uncertainty and errors. For simple engraving, clear example photos and a font sample may be enough. A live text preview suits names and messages, while a full product designer is worth it only when customers need to arrange text and images themselves.

### Can I refuse returns on personalised products?

Many stores restrict change-of-mind returns on personalised items, but you must state the policy clearly before purchase and still put right items that are defective, damaged or not as ordered. India's e-commerce rules require return, refund and cancellation information to be displayed clearly. Take legal advice on your exact wording.

### How do I avoid spelling mistakes on personalised orders?

Use specific field labels, show limits and a live preview, add a spelling confirmation tick box, repeat the personalisation in the cart and confirmation email, and allow a short window for corrections before production. For high-value items, send a proof for approval before production starts.
